reason: The sources provide over a dozen cross-corroborated facts detailing Rosetta's 10-year flight, historic orbit, lander deployment, and dramatic comet touchdown.
story: In March 2004, the European Space Agency launched Rosetta on an audacious 1.3-billion-euro expedition to chase down Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. After a decade-long trek through deep space powered by four planetary gravity assists at Earth and Mars, Rosetta made history in August 2014 by becoming the first spacecraft ever to enter orbit around a comet nucleus. Arriving at the bizarre, rubber-duck-shaped cosmic wanderer, Rosetta mapped cliffs and active gas vents before deploying its companion lander, Philae. Although Philae bounced twice and went silent within days, Rosetta escorted the comet around the Sun, discovering molecular oxygen in its coma. But as the comet drifted outbound toward Jupiter, dwindling solar light starved the probe of power. Instead of letting Rosetta freeze in darkness, scientists commanded a slow-motion dive, ending the twelve-year voyage on September 30, 2016, by touching down on the comet at a gentle walking pace.
angle: After a 10-year chase across four billion miles of space, humanity's first comet orbiter ended its mission by deliberately crash-landing onto the comet at a gentle walking pace of just two miles per hour.

claims.claim: Rosetta launched on 2 March 2004 on an Ariane 5 rocket.
The spacecraft launched from the spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana.
The Rosetta mission was developed and operated by the European Space Agency (ESA).
The total cost of the Rosetta mission was approximately 1.3 billion euros.
Flight operations for the spacecraft were managed from the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) in Darmstadt, Germany.
Rosetta's target destination was Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko.
Rosetta performed gravity assist flybys of Earth and Mars to build up the necessary velocity to reach the comet.
Rosetta's third and final Earth flyby in November 2009 brought it to a closest approach of 2,481 kilometres above the surface.
During its cruise through the asteroid belt, Rosetta performed a close flyby of the asteroid 21 Lutetia in July 2010.
Rosetta rendezvoused with Comet 67P in August 2014 after a 10-year interplanetary voyage.
Rosetta became the first spacecraft in history to orbit a comet nucleus.
Close-range imagery revealed the comet nucleus had an irregular, two-lobed structure widely compared to a rubber duck.
The spacecraft carried a piggybacked surface lander module named Philae.
Rosetta deployed Philae to attempt the first soft landing on a comet nucleus in November 2014.
Philae bounced twice on the comet's low-gravity surface before coming to rest against a cliff face.
Philae's surface science mission ceased after only a few days when its batteries ran out of power.
Instruments aboard Rosetta discovered unexpected amounts of free molecular oxygen in the coma surrounding the comet.
Because Comet 67P was heading toward the orbit of Jupiter, declining solar power made it impossible for the solar-powered orbiter to continue operating indefinitely.
Rosetta ended its mission on 30 September 2016 by making a controlled descent directly onto the comet's surface.
Rosetta touched down in the Ma'at region on the comet's head.
Rosetta impacted the surface of the comet at walking speed, calculated at approximately 2 mph (about 1 metre per second).

disputed: Exact duration of Philae battery life: S1 states 'two days later' in one section and 'after three days' in another; S4 states 'after three days'; S6 notes 'surviving just a few days'. Scripts should say 'within a few days' or 'two to three days'.

Origin of terrestrial water: S1 notes that early Rosetta data showing a deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio three times that of Earth was updated by a 2024 reanalysis finding Earth-like ratios. A script should avoid claiming definitively whether comet 67P matches Earth's oceans without qualifying the evolving analysis.
